items.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
items.snippet: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.

items.snippet: Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

items.snippet: Archaeologists found a small cemetery full of high-status burials, two of which may be the graves of Germanic chieftains.

items.title: NASA's destroyed Swift Observatory took one of the best-ever photos of bright Andromeda
items.snippet: NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

items.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

items.title: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
items.snippet: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster. Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.

items.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
items.snippet: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

items.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
items.snippet: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

items.title: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
items.snippet: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. items.title: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
items.snippet: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

items.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

items.title: 100 buses long: Scientists map one of the world's largest known coral colonies
items.snippet: A huge coral colony stretching more than 1.5 kilometers (0.93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been identified by researchers, making it one of the largest known coral colonies ever recorded.

items.title: New species of ground-dwelling bird, the largest of its kind, identified in same cave as Homo floresiensis
items.snippet: In 2009, researchers working in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island came across a leg bone. The 190,000–120,000-year-old fossil was identified as a bird bone and set aside. Like many bird bones before it, it was overlooked and left to collect dust.

items.title: Game theory helps SETI search for alien civilizations
items.snippet: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun-like stars for signs of intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

items.title: 'Stupendously large' primordial black holes ruled out as a dark matter source
items.snippet: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. If they exist, their dramatic origins would set them apart from the black holes we see today, which form when massive stars collapse. items.title: Chimp sanctuary delivers an ape's food by drone amid Florida floods
items.snippet: A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary had to deliver food to one of its 200 apes by drone this week because the property was swamped by heavy rain. But the animals stayed safe, and the water finally was receding significantly on Saturday, the organization said.
